meta.titre: Enzymes and Food Tests: optimum conditions and the laboratory reagents
meta.sous_theme: Properties of enzymes, effect of temperature, and the chemical tests for food substances

sections.contenu_markdown:
In the school laboratory in Kumba, a student mixes saliva with starch and tests drops with iodine at intervals. The blue-black colour fades faster in a warm water bath than in a cold one, and not at all in boiling water.
The same ideas help to explain why food in a fridge keeps longer.
The GCE examiners ask you to interpret temperature graphs and to describe how to test foods, often in the same paper, so both belong in one lesson.

items: Digestion breaks down large food molecules into small soluble ones.
Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are the main organic nutrients.
Reaction rate means how fast a reaction takes place.

sections.contenu_markdown:
### Enzymes
**Enzymes** are protein molecules that act as biological catalysts: they speed up chemical reactions in living things and are not used up. Each enzyme is specific and acts on one kind of substrate, such as amylase on starch, protease on proteins and lipase on fats.

**Temperature.** The rate rises as the temperature rises, because the molecules move faster and collide more often. It reaches a maximum at the **optimum temperature**. Above it the enzyme is damaged, its shape changes and it is **denatured**, so the rate falls quickly. Denaturation is permanent, whereas at very low temperatures an enzyme is only slowed down and works again when warmed. The enzymes of the human body work best at about 37 °C. The same pattern holds for the enzymes that control photosynthesis, so a graph of photosynthesis against temperature has a peak.

**pH.** Each enzyme has an optimum pH. Pepsin works best in the acid of the stomach, while amylase in saliva works best near neutral.

### Tests for food substances
| Food | Test | Positive result |
|---|---|---|
| Starch | Add iodine solution | Brown or yellow changes to blue-black |
| Reducing sugar | Add Benedict's solution and heat in a hot water bath | Blue changes through green and yellow to a brick-red precipitate |
| Protein | Add sodium hydroxide, then a few drops of dilute copper(II) sulphate (biuret test) | Blue changes to purple or violet |
| Fat | Shake the food with ethanol, then pour into water (emulsion test) | A cloudy white emulsion forms |
| Vitamin C | Add to blue DCPIP solution | The blue colour disappears |

Always state the reagent, the conditions (such as heating) and the colour change.

variantes.nom: Reading a graph of the effect of temperature
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question gives a curve of rate against temperature and asks about a labelled point
variantes.contenu_markdown: Describe the shape in three parts. Rising part: the rate increases as the temperature rises because the molecules gain kinetic energy and collide more often. Peak: the optimum temperature, where the enzyme works fastest. Falling part: the enzyme is denatured, its active site loses shape, and the substrate no longer fits. A peak always means 'optimum temperature', so say so in your answer.

variantes.nom: Testing a sample of unknown food
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks how to find out which nutrients are in a food
variantes.contenu_markdown: Crush the food, mix it with water and divide it into portions. Test each portion with a different reagent. To find sucrose (a non-reducing sugar), first boil the sample with dilute hydrochloric acid, neutralise it with sodium hydrogencarbonate, then do the Benedict's test: a colour change after this treatment but not before shows that sucrose was present.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A student mixes amylase solution with starch in five tubes kept at different temperatures. Every minute a drop is taken from each tube and added to iodine. The time taken for the blue-black colour to disappear is: 10 °C, 20 min; 20 °C, 10 min; 30 °C, 5 min; 40 °C, 4 min; 50 °C, 8 min. At 60 °C the colour was still blue-black after 30 minutes.

(a) Calculate the rate as $\dfrac{1}{\text{time}}$ in min$^{-1}$ for 10 to 50 °C.
(b) At which of the temperatures tested does the enzyme work fastest?
(c) Explain the result at 60 °C.

etapes.justification: A shorter time means a faster reaction.
The enzyme works fastest where the rate is highest.
The question needs the pattern, not just the best value.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The rate rises from 10 to 40 °C then falls at 50 °C.

etapes.justification: A starch that stays blue-black shows that the starch was not digested.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The amylase was denatured by the high temperature, so its shape changed and it could no longer act on starch.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.25 and 0.125 min$^{-1}$. (b) 40 °C, the fastest of those tested, so the optimum is close to 40 °C. (c) At 60 °C the enzyme was denatured, so no starch was digested.

items.erreur_markdown: Enzymes are killed at high temperatures.
items.pourquoi_faux: Enzymes are not living things; they are proteins. They are denatured, not killed.
items.correction_markdown: High temperatures denature enzymes, which changes their shape so that they no longer work.

items.pourquoi_faux: At low temperatures enzymes are only inactive or slow. When warmed, they work again.
items.correction_markdown: Low temperature slows an enzyme; high temperature denatures it permanently.

items.erreur_markdown: Benedict's solution is added cold, and a blue-black colour shows reducing sugar.
items.pourquoi_faux: Benedict's solution must be heated, and a brick-red precipitate shows reducing sugar. Blue-black is the iodine test for starch.
items.correction_markdown: Reducing sugar: heat with Benedict's solution, brick-red precipitate. Starch: iodine, blue-black.

items.erreur_markdown: The peak of the curve shows the temperature at which the enzyme is destroyed.
items.pourquoi_faux: The peak shows the optimum temperature, where the rate is highest. Denaturation happens above the peak.
items.correction_markdown: The peak is the optimum temperature.

items.enonce_markdown:
A student tests four foods and records the results.

(a) Sample P gives a blue-black colour with iodine.
(b) Sample Q gives a brick-red precipitate when heated with Benedict's solution.
(c) Sample R turns purple with sodium hydroxide and copper(II) sulphate.
(d) Sample S gives a cloudy white emulsion when shaken with ethanol and poured into water.

State the food substance present in each.

Liver contains catalase, which breaks down hydrogen peroxide and releases oxygen. A student collected 12 cm³ of oxygen in 2 minutes at 20 °C and 30 cm³ in 2 minutes at 37 °C. At 70 °C no gas was collected.

(a) Calculate the rate of oxygen production at 20 °C and at 37 °C in cm³ per minute.
(b) Explain the result at 70 °C.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) 20 °C: $12 \div 2 =$ **6 cm³ per minute**. 37 °C: $30 \div 2 =$ **15 cm³ per minute**.
(b) At 70 °C the catalase was denatured, so its shape was changed and it could not break down the hydrogen peroxide.

items.enonce_markdown:
A student boils some amylase solution for five minutes, then cools it to 37 °C and adds it to starch. Another sample of amylase is kept in an ice bath for five minutes, warmed to 37 °C and added to starch. The starch is digested only by the second sample.

Explain this result.
items.solution_markdown:
The enzyme was **denatured** by boiling. The shape of the active site was changed permanently, so after cooling the starch no longer fitted the enzyme and it was not digested.
In the ice bath the enzyme was only **inactive** because the molecules moved slowly. It kept its shape, so when warmed to 37 °C it worked again and digested the starch.

items_markdown: Enzymes are protein catalysts: they speed up reactions, are specific and are not used up.
Rate rises to an optimum temperature, then falls because the enzyme is denatured; cold only slows an enzyme.
A peak on a rate-temperature graph, including photosynthesis, is the optimum temperature.
Starch: iodine, blue-black. Reducing sugar: Benedict's, heat, brick-red. Protein: biuret, purple. Fat: ethanol emulsion, cloudy white.
Rate $= \dfrac{1}{\text{time taken}}$, or volume of product divided by time.
